content: Garlic, scientifically known as Allium sativum, belongs to the onion family Alliaceae. It is closely related to onions, shallots, and leeks. Throughout recorded history, garlic has been utilized for both culinary and medicinal purposes. Its flavor is characteristically pungent and sharp when raw, but it becomes milder and sweeter when cooked. The most commonly used part of the garlic plant is the bulb, which is composed of multiple individual cloves. The leaves and stems are also edible, particularly when they are young and tender. Elephant garlic, despite its name, is a different species and is actually a type of leek. Origin and Distribution The exact ancestry of cultivated garlic is uncertain due to the sterility of its cultivars, making it difficult to identify its wild progenitor. However, it is believed that garlic likely descended from Allium longicuspis, a species native to southwestern Asia. Wild garlic species, such as Allium ursinum (wild garlic), Allium vineale (crow garlic), and Allium oleraceum (field garlic), are found in Britain. In North America, Allium vineale (wild or crow garlic) and Allium canadense (meadow or wild garlic) are common weeds in fields. Culinary Uses Garlic is widely used worldwide for its strong flavor, either as a seasoning or condiment. Its flavor profile can vary depending on the method of preparation, ranging from intense when raw to mellow when cooked. Garlic is often paired with onions, tomatoes, or ginger in cooking. The papery skin of garlic cloves is typically removed before use, although whole heads of garlic can be roasted in the oven, softening the cloves for easy extraction. Garlic-infused oils are popular, but homemade versions must be stored properly to prevent botulism. Refrigeration and consumption within one week are recommended, and commercial products often include additives to reduce this risk. In Chinese cuisine, young garlic bulbs are pickled in a mixture of sugar, salt, and spices. In Russia and the Caucasus, garlic shoots are pickled and consumed as appetizers. Immature garlic scapes, also known as garlic spears or tops, are tender and have a milder flavor than cloves. They are often stir-fried or prepared like asparagus. Garlic leaves are a common vegetable in many Asian cuisines, such as Chinese, Vietnamese, Cambodian, and Korean dishes, where they are stir-fried with eggs, meat, or vegetables. Garlic is also a key ingredient in Mediterranean dishes, such as aioli (a garlic and olive oil emulsion) and skordalia (a garlic-based dip). French garlic soup, known as le tourin, is another example of its culinary versatility. Storage Garlic is best stored in a warm (above 18°C) and dry environment to prevent sprouting. Traditionally, garlic is hung, and softneck varieties are often braided into strands called plaits. Commercially, garlic is stored at 0°C in dry conditions. Historical Use Garlic has been consumed as food since ancient times. It was part of the diet of the Israelites in Egypt and was provided to laborers building the pyramids. Ancient Greek and Roman soldiers, sailors, and rural populations also consumed garlic. Galen, a prominent physician, referred to garlic as the rustic's theriac (a cure-all). In the 12th century, Alexander Neckam recommended garlic as a remedy for sun exposure during field labor. During the early 20th century, garlic was sometimes used to treat pulmonary tuberculosis. While garlic was rare in traditional English cuisine, it has been a staple in Mediterranean Europe. In ancient Greek culture, garlic was offered as a supper for Hecate at crossroads, and the Egyptians invoked garlic and onions as deities during oaths. Medicinal Use and Health Benefits Garlic has been used for thousands of years as both food and medicine. It is claimed to help prevent cardiovascular diseases, such as atherosclerosis, high cholesterol, and hypertension, as well as certain cancers. Animal studies and some early human studies suggest potential cardiovascular benefits. For example, a Czech study found that garlic supplementation reduced cholesterol accumulation on vascular walls in animals. Another study showed that garlic extract inhibited vascular calcification in humans with high cholesterol. However, a 2007 NIH-funded clinical trial found no significant effect of garlic on cholesterol levels in patients with moderately high baseline levels, highlighting the need for rigorous research. Garlic is also believed to have antimicrobial properties, as observed by Louis Pasteur in 1858. It was used as an antiseptic during World War I and II to prevent gangrene. Traditional British herbalism used garlic for hoarseness and coughs, while the Cherokee used it as an expectorant. Garlic has been shown to reduce platelet aggregation and hyperlipidemia and may help regulate blood sugar levels. Aged garlic extracts have been found to lower blood homocysteine levels and prevent some complications of diabetes. However, individuals taking insulin should consult a physician before consuming medicinal amounts of garlic. Fresh, uncooked garlic is necessary to retain its active compound, allicin. Garlic may also possess anticancer properties due to allylic sulfur compounds like diallyl disulfide (DADS). In modern naturopathy, garlic is used to treat intestinal worms and other parasites, as well as infections, digestive disorders, and fungal infections like thrush. Garlic supplementation in rats has been shown to boost testosterone levels when combined with a high-protein diet. Properties When crushed, garlic produces allicin, a potent antibiotic and antifungal compound. It also contains alliin, ajoene, enzymes, vitamin B, minerals, and flavonoids. The sharp flavor of garlic is due to sulfur-containing compounds released when its cells are damaged. These compounds are believed to have evolved as a defense mechanism against herbivores. Among the onion family, garlic has the highest concentration of these compounds, making it more potent than onions, shallots, or leeks. Cooking garlic removes allicin, reducing its spiciness. Consuming large amounts of garlic can result in its sulfur compounds being metabolized into allyl methyl sulfide (AMS), which is excreted through the lungs and skin, causing garlic breath. This effect can last for hours and is only temporarily masked by eating parsley. Superstition and Mythology Garlic has been associated with both good and evil forces. A Christian myth suggests that garlic grew from Satan's left footprint after he left the Garden of Eden. In European folklore, garlic was used for protection against demons, werewolves, and vampires. It was believed that wearing garlic or hanging it in windows could ward off vampires. This association may stem from garlic's antimicrobial properties, which could prevent infections leading to delusions and mental illness. Cautions Adverse effects of garlic include halitosis, indigestion, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Garlic should not be taken with warfarin, antiplatelets, saquinavir, antihypertensives, or hypoglycemic drugs. Garlic-in-oil preparations can cause botulism if not stored properly. Adding acid and refrigerating can reduce this risk. While culinary quantities are safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding, large amounts of garlic or supplements may increase the risk of bleeding and could potentially cause miscarriage. Some breastfeeding mothers have reported their babies being slow to feed and emitting a garlic odor. The long-term effects of garlic supplementation are largely unknown, but garlic has been consumed for thousands of years without significant adverse effects. Topical application of raw garlic can cause serious burns, especially in children. It is strongly discouraged to apply raw garlic to the skin or insert it into body cavities.
